newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Political, financial troubles slam South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Political, financial troubles slam South Korea.

text.p: South Korean business suffered a fresh blow on Wednesday on a newspaper report that prosecutors were probing the 16th ranked Hansol Group in connection with a scandal swirling around President Kim Young-sam's son.
The Chosun Ilbo reported that state prosecutors had evidence that the group managed a seven billion won ($7.8 million) fund on behalf of an associate of Kim Hyun-chul.
The Hansol Group, whose flagship Hansol Paper is the country's largest paper manufacturer, issued a vaguely-worded statement apparently in response to the report.

"Talk about an influx of funds into the Hansol Group is not true," the statement quoted group information director Kim Jung-bo as saying. "There seems to be a big misunderstanding. I hope the prosecution will uncover the truth."
Kim is being investigated by prosecutors for his involvement in a loans-for-kickbacks scandal involving a failed steelmaker, Hanbo Steel Co.
Domestic newspapers have quoted prosecutors as saying Kim Hyun-chul will be arrested soon.
The Chosun Ilbo report sent shares of all seven of the group's listed companies tumbling.
Hansol Paper had slipped 1,500 won to 19,800 and Hansol Electron had fallen 1,900 won to 22,400 in late morning trading. Hansol Merchant Bank had slipped 300 won to 8,900.

Hansol Telecommunication was off 3,400 won to 48,500, Hansol Chemical was off 1,500 to 23,300, Hansol Paperboard had slipped 200 won to 5,800 and Hansol CSN was down 1,200 won to 29,100 in late morning trading.
The Korea Composite Stock Price Index stood at 693.82 points, down 7.75 points or 1.10 percent late on Wednesday morning.
Some analysts said the group could be in for a beating.
"This has been around as a rumour for a long time," said Y.K. Pak, paper industry analyst at ING Barings. "We have to wait to see if other details come out. But this is really negative."
Others said Hansol share prices would rebound quickly.
"The negative impact is not likely to last long as prosecutors' investigation will not badly damage business activities of the group," said Chang Kun-woo of Daishin Securities.
There was other bad news as well.
Yu Sung Co Ltd, one of the country's largest manufacturers of woollen textiles, said on Tuesday it had defaulted on payments of 227 million won. It said it would seek court protection on Wednesday.
The Korea Stock Exchange indefinitely halted trading of Yu Sung shares from Wednesday morning.
Corporate bankruptcies are becoming more common in South Korea as the government seeks to end its practice of shielding companies from failure.
Hanbo Steel collapsed in January, followed by Sammi Steel Co in March. The Jinro Group avoided collapse last month only after banks agreed to a rescue.
The Ssangyong and Doosan groups have announced restructuring plans in recent weeks. Both have said they will sell real estate and merge or sell affiliates.
